==English==

===Etymology 1===
From {{inh|en|enm|dull}}, {{m|enm|dul}} (also {{m|enm|dyll}}, {{m|enm|dill}}, {{m|enm|dwal}}), from {{inh|en|ang|dol|t=dull, foolish, erring, heretical; foolish, silly; presumptuous}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*dol}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*dulaz}}, from earlier {{m|gem-pro|*dwulaz}}, a variant of {{m|gem-pro|*dwalaz|t=stunned, mad, foolish, misled}}, from {{inh|en|ine-pro|*dʰwel-}}, {{m|ine-pro|*dʰewel-|t=to dim, dull, cloud, make obscure, swirl, whirl}}. 

Cognate with {{cog|sco|dull}}, {{m|sco|doll||slow to understand or hear, deaf, dull}}, {{cog|frr|dol||rash, unthinking, giddy, flippant}}, {{cog|nl|dol||crazy, mad, insane}}, {{cog|nds|dul}}, {{m|nds|dol||mad, silly, stupid, fatuous}}, {{cog|de|toll||crazy, mad, wild, fantastic}}, {{cog|da|dval||foolish, absurd}}, {{cog|is|dulur||secretive, silent}}, [[West Flemish|West-Flemish]] ''dul'' (angry, furious).

====Alternative forms====
* {{l|en|dul}}, {{l|en|dulle}} {{qualifier|both obsolete}}

====Pronunciation====
* {{IPA|en|/dʌl/|a=RP,GA}}
** {{audio|en|en-us-dull.ogg|a=US}}
** {{audio|en|LL-Q1860 (eng)-Back ache-dull.wav|a=UK}}
* {{IPA|en|/dʊl/|a=Northern England}}
* {{rhymes|en|ʌl|s=1}}

====Adjective====
{{en-adj|er}}

# Lacking the ability to [[cut]] easily; not [[sharp]].
#: {{synonyms|en|blunt}}
#: {{antonyms|en|sharp}}
#: {{ux|en|All these knives are '''dull'''.}}
# {{cap|boring}}; not [[exciting]] or [[interesting]].
#: {{synonyms|en|Thesaurus:boring}}
#: {{ux|en|He sat through the '''dull''' lecture and barely stayed awake.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1895|author=S. R. Crockett|title=A Cry Across the Black Water
|passage="You are very '''dull''' this morning, Sheriff," said the youngest daughter of the house, who, being the baby and pretty, had grown pettishly privileged in speech.}}
# Not [[shiny]]; having a [[matte]] finish or no particular [[luster]] or brightness.
#: {{synonyms|en|lackluster|matte|Thesaurus:dim}}
#: {{antonyms|en|bright}}
#: {{ux|en|Choose a '''dull''' finish to hide fingerprints.}}
#: ''a '''dull''' fire or lamp;  a '''dull''' red or yellow;  {{nowrap|a '''dull'''}} mirror''
#* {{RQ:Belloc Lowndes Lodger|I|0016
|passage=A great bargain also had been the excellent Axminster carpet which covered the floor; as, again, the arm-chair in which Bunting now sat forward, staring into the '''dull''', small fire.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1959|author=Robert Adams Wilson|title=Bird Islands of New Zealand|page=67
|passage=The young bird had the plumage of the saddleback, not the even chestnut of the jackbird, although its plumage was rather '''duller''' than that of the adult.}}
# Not [[bright]] or [[intelligent]]; stupid; having slow understanding.
#: {{synonyms|en|Thesaurus:stupid}}
#: {{antonyms|en|Thesaurus:intelligent}}
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Merchant of Venice|act=III|scene=ii|passage=She is not bred so '''dull''' but she can learn.}}
#* {{RQ:Thackeray Vanity Fair|chapter=5|passage='''dull''' at classical learning}}
#* {{RQ:Allingham China Governess|chapter=15|passage=She paused and took a defiant breath. ‘If you don't believe me, I can't help it. But I'm not a liar.’ ¶ ‘No,’ said Luke, grinning at her. ‘You're not '''dull''' enough! {{...}} What about the kid's clothes? I don't suppose they were anything to write home about, but didn't you keep anything? A bootee or a bit of embroidery or anything at all?’}}
# {{cap|sluggish}}, [[listless]].
#: {{syn|en|ponderous|slothful|Thesaurus:lazy|Thesaurus:slow}}
#* {{RQ:KJV|Matthew|13|xiii|text=This people's heart is waxed gross, and their ears are '''dull''' of hearing.}}
#* {{RQ:Spenser Faerie Queene|text=O, help my weak wit and sharpen my '''dull''' tongue.}}
#* {{RQ:Maxwell Mirror and the Lamp|chapter=7|passage={{...}} St. Bede's at this period of its history was perhaps the poorest and most miserable parish in the East End of London. Close-packed, crushed by the buttressed height of the railway viaduct, rendered airless by huge walls of factories, it at once banished lively interest from a stranger's mind and left only a '''dull''' oppression of the spirit.}}
# {{cap|bored}}, [[depressed]], [[down]].
#: {{syn|en|Thesaurus:be bored|Thesaurus:sad}}
#: {{ux|en|I felt '''dull''' all day.}}
# {{cap|cloudy}}, [[overcast]].
#: {{ux|en|It's a '''dull''' day.}}
# {{cap|insensible}}; [[unfeeling]].
#: {{syn|en|emotionless|Thesaurus:alexithymic}}
#* {{RQ:Beaumont Fletcher Comedies and Tragedies|The Knight of Malta|5|2|passage=Think me not / So '''dull''' a devil to forget the loss / Of such a matchless wife.}}
# {{cap|heavy}}; [[lifeless]]; [[inert]].
#: {{syn|en|immobile|Thesaurus:inactive|Thesaurus:stationary}}
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Two Gentlemen of Verona|IV|ii|passage=the '''dull''' earth}}
#* ''c. 1857''', {{w|Henry Wadsworth Longfellow}}, ''Table-Talk''
# {{lb|en|of pain etc}} Not [[intense]]; felt [[indistinct]]ly or only [[slight]]ly.
#: {{ux|en|Pressing on the bruise produces a '''dull''' pain.}}
# Not [[clear]], [[muffled]]. {{q|of a noise or sound}}

====Verb====
{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|transitive}} To render dull; to remove or [[blunt]] an edge or something that was sharp.
#: {{ux|en|Years of misuse have '''dulled''' the tools.}}
#* {{RQ:Bacon War with Spain|passage=This {{...}} '''dulled''' their swords.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To soften, [[moderate]] or [[blunt]]; to make dull, stupid, or sluggish; to [[stupefy]].
#: {{ux|en|He drinks to '''dull''' the pain.}}
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Cymbeline|I|vi|passage=Those [drugs] she has / Will stupefy and '''dull''' the sense a while.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1850|author=w:Richard Chenevix Trench|title=Notes on the Miracles of Our Lord
|passage=Use and custom have so '''dulled''' our eyes.}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To lose a [[sharp]] edge; to become dull.
#: {{ux|en|A razor will '''dull''' with use.}}
# To render dim or obscure; to sully; to tarnish.

===Etymology 2===
Probably from {{bor|en|ga|dul}}, {{m|ga|dol||loop, noose, snare}}.

====Pronunciation====
* {{IPA|en|/dʌl/|a=GA}}
* {{IPA|en|/dʌl/|/dul/|a=Ireland}}<ref>Michael Traynor, ''The English Dialect of Donegal'' (1953).</ref>

====Noun====
{{en-noun}}

# {{lb|en|Ireland|Southern US|now|rare|or|obsolete}} A [[noose]] of string, metal wire, or hair used to [[snare]] an animal, especially a [[fish]].
#* {{quote-journal|en|year=1903|journal=Field and Stream|page=66
|passage=Play fair, boys. No dynamite nor "dulling." The deadly "'''dull'''," or wire noose, is a fatal weapon against a trout.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|date=June 1 1929|title=Southern Agriculturist|volume=59|page=8|chapter=Notes from a Farmer's Experience
|passage=A horse with long, stiff hair in the tail was selected. {{...}} a quick jerk [...] secured the material for a "'''dull'''." {{...}} Then the "'''dull'''" was ready for use. {{...}} the noose [was] slipped over the head to the gills and then with a quick jerk the sucker was dulled and pulled out of the water. Generally the '''dull''' held the fish and it was loosened and dropped on the bank but sometimes it was thrown out of the water but then slipped loose from the '''dull''' and fell on one of the banks or, worse luck, into the water. {{...}}}}

=====Further reading=====
* '''1953''', Michael Traynor, ''The English Dialect of Donegal'', page 91: "''Dull'' (Dŭhl, dül), ''n., v.'' Also in form ''dool''. 1. ''n.'' A loop, noose of rope or cord (McD. L. OB); esp. a running knot (MacI); a snare. In fishing with drag-nets the term "completing the dull" (making the loop complete) is used on L. Swilly (H). 2. ''v.'' To loop. ''Dull that rope round the tree.'' Hence ''i.'' ''Dulling'', ''vbl. n.'', a method of catching sheep by means of a noose. When a sheep has got into a fix upon cliffs and cannot be climbed to, the best cliff-man goes out provided with a noose [...] and gets the loop round some part of the sheep, pulls the slip-knot taut and hauls out the sheep. This is called dulling sheep and is a regular art at Hornhead; {{...}}"
* '''2011''', Diarmaid Ó Muirithe, ''Words We Don't Use (Much Anymore)'': "I heard ''dulling'' from a sheepman at the bottom of Errigal mountain, a method of catching sheep stuck in a ravine by means of a noose."

====Verb====
{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|Ireland|Southern US|now|rare|or|obsolete}} To [[fish]] (or [[snare]] an animal, especially a fish) with such a noose.
#* {{quote-journal|en|date=March 11 1880|journal=Forest and Stream
|passage=I hope that the barbarous practice called '''''dulling''''' has gone out of fashion.}}
#* {{quote-journal|en|year=1903|journal=Field and Stream|page=66
|passage=Play fair, boys. No dynamite nor "'''dulling'''." The deadly "dull," or wire noose, is a fatal weapon against a trout.}}
#* {{quote-journal|en|year=1915|title=Clare Island Survey: A Biological Survey of Clare Island|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy|page=21
|passage=In Irish-English, “'''dulling''' for trout” is well known,—the fish as they lie still in a pool are snared with a noose of horsehair.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|date=June 1 1929|title=Southern Agriculturist|volume=59|page=8|chapter=Notes from a Farmer's Experience
|passage=While I was having my fishing experience on a West Virginia stream I did not realize that it was unique so far as average American boys are concerned. In those boyhood days we went "'''dulling'''" for suckers in the small creek that crossed my father's farm. {{...}} To '''dull''' suckers the water had to be clear {{...}} the noose [was] slipped over the head to the gills and then with a quick jerk the sucker was '''dulled''' and pulled out of the water. {{...}} At any rate my nephews have not practiced '''dulling''' suckers to anything like the extent that their father and uncle did.}}
